To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of QACs in the hospital and in the environment is widespread, that QACs are not considered to be antibiotics and are not included in susceptibility tests for antibiotics, that QAC resistance is not included in antibiotic susceptibility breakpoints, and that the impact of QAC use on the emergence of resistance to antibiotics is not yet fully understood.
QACs have been used for decades, and that they are still used in hospitals, industry, cosmetics, and in households.

(i) there is a lack in the literature of standardised procedures to interpret susceptibility test results; (ii) there is a need to define resistance to QACs, to establish epidemiological cut-off and clinical resistance breakpoints; (iii) QACs may select for multiple-antibiotics resistant organisms, and (iv) the design of international guidance on the use of QACs is needed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of QAC use on antibiotic resistance.
the impact of the use of QACs in hospitals on antibiotic resistance.
the impact of QAC use on the emergence of resistance to antibacterials and the potential impact of such resistance on human health.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

QACs have the potential to select for antibiotic resistance in the environment and in patients, but this potential is not yet sufficiently documented to be able to make a clear recommendation on QAC use.
QACs have a selective effect on microflora and may be involved in the emergence of antibiotic resistant organisms.
QACs are not the main cause of the emergence of antibiotic resistances.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is an urgent need for standardised susceptibility testing methods, epidemiological cut-off points and clinical breakpoints.
the potential of QACS for selecting antibiotic resistance should not be ignored.
the use of QACs should be restricted in order to avoid their contribution to the emergence of resistance to antibiotics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the potential of QACS to select for antibiotic resistance in the clinical and non-clinical environment needs to be addressed.
the potential for QACs to select for multiple-antibacterial-resistant organisms is real, and it is time to address this issue.
QACs are not innocuous and should be handled with caution.
